seo.title: Karmic tail 9 12 3 compatibility: what it means for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 9 12 3 compatibility: a couple hides what is most real, lives on "almost" for years and learns to give love a visible home. With a worked example.

title: Karmic tail 9-12-3 in compatibility: a secret union in search of a home of its own
short: The Hermit walks away from people, The Empress is the fullness of earthly life itself, and between them hangs The Hanged Man, who is going nowhere. In the couple's tail 9-12-3 these cards add up to a single plot, and Chekhov wrote it down long ago in "The Lady with the Dog": two people find in each other what is most real, hide it from the world and live for years with the feeling that "in a little while the solution would be found". The tail says what such a couple has to learn: to bring the secret into the light and give their love a visible shape.

sections.h2: A story that follows the three cards
paragraphs: "The Lady with the Dog" appeared in December 1899 in the magazine Russkaya Mysl (Russian Thought). Chekhov made the first note for it back in 1896 in Kislovodsk, just three words: "The lady with the pug". The story was written after a break of almost a year: Chekhov had just finished building his house in Yalta and was growing close to the actress Olga Knipper.

The plot is well known. In Yalta a Muscovite, Dmitri Gurov, meets Anna Sergeyevna, a visitor from the town of S. Both are married. The holiday romance ought to end at the station, but it does not: in winter Gurov travels to S., and then for years she comes to see him in Moscow, at the Slaviansky Bazaar hotel. The story breaks off in the middle of a conversation about how they are to live from now on.

Laid out along the couple's tail, it falls into three acts in exactly the order of the cards. Yalta and Oreanda are The Hermit: two people leave the crowd and are silent together. The Moscow winter and the years of secret meetings are The Hanged Man: a life suspended between two towns. The last sentence is The Empress, who never arrives: "a new and splendid life".

There is a clue in the words as well. Early in the story Gurov knows from experience that "with decent people, especially Moscow people — always slow to move and irresolute — every intimacy... inevitably grows into a regular problem of extreme intricacy". Garnett's "problem" stands for the Russian zadacha, which also means "task". The last words of the story say that "the most complicated and difficult part of it was only just beginning". The story opens with the word "task" and ends where the main task begins. **In Lisovskaya's method the couple's tail is precisely the line of tasks.**

One caveat, without which the plot would be misread. Chekhov's lovers are held by two other marriages. Tail 9-12-3 says nothing about third parties, infidelity or secret affairs. It speaks about a form of life — a union where what is most real is hidden and what is visible is postponed. A real couple's cages are of a different kind: two towns, two jobs, a parents' flat, "once we're on our feet", the habit of living as guests in each other's lives.

sections.h2: Entry to the task — The Hermit: two people silent above the sea
paragraphs: The key scene of the Yalta part is not the kiss on the pier but the dawn at Oreanda: "At Oreanda they sat on a seat not far from the church, looked down at the sea, and were silent. Yalta was hardly visible through the morning mist; white clouds stood motionless on the mountain-tops." Two people up high, below them a town they can barely see. A man walks up — "probably a keeper" — looks at them and walks away, and even "this detail seemed mysterious and beautiful, too".

This is the entry to the task: what the couple wants together. The Hermit at this point is the wish for a world of their own where outsiders do not come; for a quiet in which nobody has to entertain anybody; for a slow pace. Lisovskaya writes that such couples take a long time over every step, from the first kiss to the wedding, show love through deeds, and tell people about events only after the fact. In Chekhov, on the very first night Gurov eats a slice of water-melon and "there followed at least half an hour of silence", and of Gurov himself we are told that with women "he was at ease with them even when he was silent".

In a couple's matrix point M does two jobs: it is the entry to the tail and the "common language" on the relationship line. So every 9-12-3 couple has The Hermit as its common language. **These two understand each other without words, and that is their strength.** The scenes are familiar: they leave the party before anyone else so they can finish the conversation at home; friends learn about the wedding from a photo; each has a corner and an evening of their own, and nobody takes offence.

But the point sits on the line of tasks, and the same wish turns into resistance. The world for two starts being guarded — first from strangers, then from difficult conversations. Gurov puts the creed into words himself: "All personal life rested on secrecy." The trouble is not the secret but what gets hidden along with it. In Gurov's life "everything that made the kernel of his life, was hidden from other people", while out in the open was "all that was false in him, the sheath in which he hid himself to conceal the truth". Waite's reversed list for The Hermit has "Concealment, disguise". A couple at this entry recognises them not in deceiving each other but in the habit of keeping the best to themselves: troubles pile up in silence, and from the outside everything looks "fine".

For Waite, The Hermit is "a card of attainment... rather than a card of quest", and not a card of escape: the man has already arrived where others are only heading. So it is with the couple. The Hermit's quiet is good while it is a common language, and bad once it becomes a way of not talking about the main thing.

sections.h2: Middle of the task — The Hanged Man: "in a little while the solution would be found"
paragraphs: In Moscow Gurov expects that "the image of Anna Sergeyevna would be shrouded in a mist in his memory", like the others before her. It is not. Anna Sergeyevna "did not visit him in dreams, but followed him about everywhere like a shadow and haunted him". Lisovskaya writes that Hanged Man couples feel each other at a distance; Chekhov shows what that looks like from inside: a man lives in one town and in his thoughts in another.

There is no one to tell. One night Gurov cannot hold back and says to his card partner, an official: "If only you knew what a fascinating woman I made the acquaintance of in Yalta!" The man gets into his sledge, turns round and replies: "You were right this evening: the sturgeon was a bit too strong!" After that Gurov feels that "in the end there is left a life grovelling and curtailed, worthless and trivial, and there is no escaping or getting away from it — just as though one were in a madhouse or a prison". Waite's reversed list for The Hanged Man has "the crowd, body politic" — society as a whole. That is exactly the life that is "exactly like the lives of his friends and acquaintances": proper on the outside and empty within.

Then come the years. Once every two or three months Anna Sergeyevna comes to Moscow and waits in her hotel room since the evening before. Gurov arrives, she cries, and he thinks: "Let her have her cry out. I'll sit down and wait," — and he rings for tea. This is what the middle of the tail looks like: not drama but routine. **Suspension becomes a way of life.**

Wen calls The Hanged Man "the unsettling calm before a storm" and compares it to the question The Fool asks: "will the Seeker fall or fly?" On the way to a rendezvous Gurov's daughter asks him: "And why are there no thunderstorms in the winter, father?" In this winter there really is no thunder. Nothing breaks and nothing forces a decision. Lisovskaya notes that Hanged Man couples need a push from outside to reach the wedding: left to themselves, they can hang as long as they like.

In a real couple the middle looks mundane. "We'll make it official once we can afford a proper wedding." "We'll move in together when this project is over." Two towns "for the time being", now into the fifth year. One partner bends their whole schedule around the other and says nothing; the other does not even know what was given up for their sake. Outside, a perfect picture; inside, tiredness and decisions made "because that's how it has to be".

There is simple arithmetic here too: 9 + 3 = 12. The middle of the tail is the entry and the task added together without reduction. The couple wants to hide and to grow at the same time, and hangs between the two wishes. And one more figure: in 87.6% of couples with this tail neither partner has The Hanged Man in their personal tail (our run through the engine). The suspension is not brought in by one of them — it is born between the two, and looking for someone to blame is pointless.

The middle has its gift as well. In the last scene Gurov sees his greying head in the mirror and understands that "he had fallen properly, really in love — for the first time in his life". He "no longer cared for arguments; he felt profound compassion". The Hanged Man changes the point of view: the two begin to see each other not as they imagined each other in Yalta. A pause works if it is lived through, not sat out.

sections.h2: Main task — The Empress: a life with no subject
paragraphs: The last paragraph of the story: "And it seemed as though in a little while the solution would be found, and then a new and splendid life would begin; and it was clear to both of them that they had still a long, long road before them, and that the most complicated and difficult part of it was only just beginning."

The verbs are worth a second look. "The solution would be found" — by whom? "A new life would begin" — on its own? **The most important sentence of the story has no one who acts.** The solution is meant to turn up, the life is meant to begin. Wen writes the exact opposite about The Empress: "She produces. She makes things happen." The Empress is a card of action; in Waite's list, next to fruitfulness, stand "action, initiative".

The couple's main task is read mostly through its minus: what does not work and what has to be learned. For tail 9-12-3 one thing does not work — the move from "would be found" to "we decided". Writing about The Empress's tasks in a couple, Lisovskaya names immaturity, the influence of relatives, money that is feast or famine, jealousy, and the lopsided union in which one grows and the other stands still. And her advice reads almost like a reply to Gurov: make the union official, learn to make decisions independently, let each find a calling of their own, speak about desires directly.

Chekhov places houses all through the story. Gurov, we are told in the first chapter, "owned two houses in Moscow". Anna Sergeyevna's husband "lived in a house of his own in Old Gontcharny Street". Each of them has a house; the couple has a hotel room. Waite's Empress is "all that is symbolized by the visible house of man". Her task for this couple lies not in walls but in visibility: there has to be somewhere the union can be seen.

A visible home takes many forms. A flat, even a rented one, with both names on the door. A shared budget instead of "my" money and "your" money. A party the two of them throw for their people. A garden, a dog, a shared venture that grows. A plan with dates instead of "some day". The Empress does not demand children and does not promise them: she is about love acquiring something that grows and can be seen.

Through the minus the task is just as recognisable. Years together — and not a single shared shelf. Jealousy flares at someone else's party, because in public the two are hardly ever a couple. One grows at work, the other waits and stores up resentment. The parents still decide where the couple sees in the New Year. This is not a verdict but a list of what to learn.

The numbers show that the task belongs to both. Tail 9-12-3 is built from six combinations of personal tails, and in all six the partners' personal karmic tasks add up to exactly 30: 21 + 9, 20 + 10, 19 + 11, 18 + 12, 17 + 13, 15 + 15. The World and The Hermit, Judgement and The Wheel of Fortune, The Sun and Strength, The Moon and The Hanged Man, The Star and Death, The Devil and The Devil. Neither of the two has The Empress as a personal task. **Thirty reduces to three: the most earthly card in the deck is one the couple only gets together.**

sections.h2: The couple's centre — The Devil: two birds in separate cages
paragraphs: The couple's centre is the atmosphere inside the union, what is not on show. In 83.9% of couples with tail 9-12-3 it holds The Devil, in 16.1% The Lovers. And Chekhov has a sentence in which both stand:

"Anna Sergeyevna and he loved each other like people very close and akin, like husband and wife, like tender friends; it seemed to them that fate itself had meant them for one another, and they could not understand why he had a wife and she a husband; and it was as though they were a pair of birds of passage, caught and forced to live in different cages."

The beginning of the sentence is The Lovers: love, choice, closeness. The end is The Devil: a fate that holds on, and cages. Back in Yalta, as she leaves, Anna Sergeyevna says: "It's the finger of destiny!" Waite's divinatory list for The Devil contains the word "fatality", followed at once by a reservation: "that which is predestined but is not for this reason evil". For the atmosphere of a couple this is an exact formula: **the bond feels inevitable, and that in itself is neither bad nor good.**

Gurov's last question is: "How could they be free from this intolerable bondage?" Constance Garnett chose the word "bondage" for the Russian puty, fetters — the very word Wen uses for The Devil: "bondage to the material and superficial". Lisovskaya, in her chapter on The Devil in a couple, arrives at the thought that nobody belongs to anybody. In its minus this atmosphere is the wish to possess, jealousy, a union held together by intimacy alone, silence about one's own desires. In its plus it is something Chekhov also recorded: "They forgave each other for what they were ashamed of in their past, they forgave everything in the present." Lisovskaya describes The Devil of a couple in its plus in almost the same words: they accept each other's dark sides and forgive mistakes.

There is a clue in the numbers, too. No birth date gives The Devil at the centre of a personal matrix: centre 15 exists only in a couple. Neither of the two brings this atmosphere in — it appears when they are together. Which means the keys to the cages are shared as well.

For couples with centre 6 the same tail sounds softer: inside there is not attachment-as-fate but love-as-choice. What matters more for them is not to take The Hermit's silence for agreement, and to choose each other out loud, again and again.

One line in earnest. The Devil at the centre speaks of the strength of a bond; it is not permission to put up with pressure, control or threats. If there is fear in the relationship, that is not a "karmic plot" but a reason to call a local emergency number or see a psychologist.

sections.h2: The couple's values: The Hermit or The Moon
paragraphs: The couple's values are its spiritual purpose, what the union exists for. With tail 9-12-3 only two cards appear here: The Hermit in 63.2% of couples and The Moon in 36.8%. Most often, in 55.4% of couples, the result is The Devil at the centre and The Hermit in the values. The union rests on a strong bond and lives for the depth the two find only in each other.

Both cards can be heard in a letter Chekhov wrote four years before the story, on 23 March 1895, to Alexei Suvorin. Suvorin had been advising him to marry. Chekhov replied: "By all means I will be married if you wish it. But on these conditions: everything must be as it has been hitherto — that is, she must live in Moscow while I live in the country, and I will come and see her. Happiness continued from day to day, from morning to morning, I cannot stand." And further: "I promise you to be a splendid husband, but give me a wife who, like the moon, won't appear in my sky every day."

This is the entry of tail 9-12-3 written down as the terms of a marriage: a world of one's own, meetings not every day, love without the everyday. And The Moon in the values turns up in it literally, as the word "moon" itself.

Six years later, on 25 May 1901, Chekhov married Olga Knipper. The same day a telegram went to his mother: "Dear Mama, give me your blessing, I am getting married. Everything will stay as it was. Leaving to drink koumiss" (our translation). **"Everything will stay as it was" is The Hermit's wish in the role of resistance:** a family begins with a promise that nothing will begin. And the story, written a year and a half earlier, ends with the words "a new and splendid life would begin". Between those two phrases lies the whole of The Empress's task.

The marriage turned out almost as the letter had planned it: she acted at the Art Theatre in Moscow, he lived in Yalta and wrote to her almost every day. Tatiana Shchepkina-Kupernik recalled that "these snatched meetings, the constant anxiety for each other, cost them both dearly" (our translation). Chekhov did not judge his characters, and nobody here judges him: it is simply that a plot, once written down, turned out to be more than literature.

And in Yalta Chekhov had a garden. Kuprin remembered him saying of it: "Before I came here all this was waste land and ravines, all covered with stones and thistles. Then I came and turned this wilderness into a cultivated, beautiful place." And adding: "in three or four hundred years all the earth will become a flourishing garden". Chekhov thought of that future, in Kuprin's words, "when, in the mornings, alone, silently, he trimmed his roses, still moist from the dew". Alone and silent — that is The Hermit. A garden that has begun to bear fruit — that is The Empress. **One picture holds the strong version of the tail: a silence that grows something.** All a 9-12-3 couple has to do is change one word: not "alone" but "together".

sections.h2: What Waite saw: the lantern, the field and the waterfall
paragraphs: The cards on this site have their own artwork; this section is about the classic deck of Waite and Pamela Colman Smith, which Waite and Wen wrote about. Its pictures hide the same clues as the story.

Waite distinguishes his Hermit from the older decks by one detail: "the lamp is not enveloped partially in the mantle of its bearer". The light is not hidden. Wen describes the Hermit as "cloaked in gray, with gray sky behind him". In Chekhov grey is the colour of the whole middle: in S., opposite Anna Sergeyevna's house, stretches "a long grey fence adorned with nails"; the hotel floor is "covered with grey army cloth", the inkstand is "grey with dust", the bed "covered by a cheap grey blanket, such as one sees in hospitals", and at the Slaviansky Bazaar Anna Sergeyevna waits "wearing his favourite grey dress".

In front of Waite's Empress "a field of corn is ripening... and beyond there is a fall of water". In Yalta Gurov and Anna Sergeyevna drive out almost every evening "to Oreanda or to the waterfall" — to the heights or to the water — and every time they return to the hotel. And in Moscow "the kernel of his life" stays hidden. **A kernel hidden from everyone, and a field that ripens in plain sight: that is the difference between the middle and the task of this tail.**

Waite calls the Hanged Man "the seeming martyr": there is a nimbus round his head, and "the tree of sacrifice is living wood, with leaves thereon". The sacrifice in this card only looks like an end. On the first night Anna Sergeyevna sits "like 'the woman who was a sinner' in an old-fashioned picture" — again a pose out of a painting, not the truth about her.

On Waite's Devil "two chains are carried to the necks of two figures, male and female". Chekhov's Russian says the birds of passage are "samets i samka", male and female; Garnett's "a pair of birds of passage" drops the detail. And Waite adds the main point: the one exalted above these two "is not to be their master for ever".
Chekhov broke the story off at the threshold. For a living couple the story goes on, and there are points where the plot can turn:

ul: **Keep the quiet, but do not hide the hard things in it.** A corner of one's own, an evening of one's own, a common language without words — that is The Hermit's plus. A hard conversation happens now, not "when the moment is right".

**Give "later" a deadline.** Say out loud what the couple is waiting for and until when. The push from outside that Hanged Man couples wait for can be chosen by the couple: a date, an application, a lease in both names.
**Make concessions shared.** If one gives something up for the other, it is a decision of both, not one person's quiet heroics.
**Write "we" into the sentence.** Not "the solution will be found" but "we decided". The Empress is a card of action.
**Give the union a visible shape.** A home with both names on the door; a shared budget; a party for their own people; a venture or a garden that grows.
**Let each partner grow.** Lisovskaya advises Empress couples that each partner find a calling of their own: a visible home is sturdier when both have a life beyond its doorstep.

paragraphs: The strong version of tail 9-12-3 is a couple that has kept its quiet without hiding in it. The hardest part turns out to be the most earthly one: not finding the solution but making it, and putting up the first shelf together.

Each point of the couple's matrix is the sum of the same points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22. The middle of a couple's tail is not recalculated from its two outer numbers: it too is added up from the partners' middles.
The first partner, 02.01.1980, has personal tail 9-3-21 and centre 6. The second, 14.09.1975, has personal tail 18-9-9 and centre 9. The couple's tail:

The couple's centre: 6 + 9 = 15, The Devil. The couple's values, recalculated from the couple's own sums, are 9, The Hermit; a plain sum of the partners' values, 9 + 9 = 18, would give The Moon, which is why a couple's values are recalculated rather than added. The middle of this couple came from one partner's Empress and the other's Hermit: 3 + 9 = 12.
Tail 9-12-3 occurs in roughly one couple in 75 — 1.334% of couples, 25th place among 97 couple tails. A pair like the one in the example is the most common of the six combinations of personal tails:

ul: 9-3-21 and 18-9-9 — 36.0% of such couples;

paragraphs: The same numbers make one more couple tail, 9-3-12, which is over seven times rarer: 0.176% of couples. There The Empress stands in the middle and The Hanged Man in the main task. A full house and a shared household are that couple's road, and what it has to learn is pausing, giving way and setting boundaries. In 9-12-3 it is the other way round: waiting is the road, the home is the task. The centre of 9-3-12 is also most often The Devil (62.7%), but The Lovers appear noticeably more often — in 37.3% of couples.

The order 9-12-3 also occurs as a personal tail — for 1,974 dates since 1900. That is a different calculation with different roles for the points: a personal tail is read about a person, a couple's tail about a union. Matching numbers do not carry the meaning across.

The telegram to Ye. Ya. Chekhova of 25 May 1901 and the words of T. L. Shchepkina-Kupernik — after the notes to Chekhov's Complete Works and Letters, Letters, vol. 10 (1981); our translation.
A. I. Kuprin, "To Chekhov's Memory" (1904), in the translation by S. S. Koteliansky and Leonard Woolf (1921).

A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910); Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015); Yuliana Lisovskaya, Matritsa sudby: sovmestimost (Destiny Matrix: Compatibility, 2024). The run through all couples is the site's engine, over every date since 1900.
**Entry to the task — 9, The Hermit.** This is the wish the couple starts from: a world for two, quiet, a slow pace, love without witnesses. Later the same wish pushes back against change.

**Middle of the task — 12, The Hanged Man.** This is how the couple lives the road: by waiting, by giving way, by a life of "for now" in which everything important is put off until some decision arrives.

**Main task — 3, The Empress.** What to learn: turning the hidden into the visible — a home, a shared household and budget, plans with dates, growth for each of the two and the fruit of a shared venture.

intro: At the centre of most such couples stands The Devil: an attachment that feels like fate. What follows is an investigation: what is written in the cards themselves, in Waite, Wen and Lisovskaya, in the numbers of the site's engine, and in a story Chekhov seems to have written from this very tail.

faq.q: What does karmic tail 9-12-3 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the task of a union in which two people easily create a secret world of their own but take a long time to give it a visible shape. The entry is The Hermit: the wish for quiet and a world for two. The middle is The Hanged Man: a life of "for now" and postponed decisions. The main task is The Empress: a home, a shared household, plans, growth for each and the fruit of a shared venture.

faq.q: Is tail 9-12-3 a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail does not predict break-ups and sets no deadlines. It shows where the couple gets stuck and what it has to learn. For 9-12-3 that is the move from "some day" to "we decided", and the move is entirely in the hands of the two.

faq.q: Is this the tail of a secret affair?
faq.a: No. "The Lady with the Dog" is here as a story about a form of life, not about infidelity. The tail does not point to third parties and says nothing about faithfulness. What such a couple keeps secret is usually the most ordinary things: plans, troubles, what the two do not show even to those close to them.

faq.q: How does the couple tail 9-12-3 differ from the personal tail 9-12-3?
faq.a: A personal tail is worked out from one date and read about a person. A couple's tail is added up from two personal matrices and read about the union: the couple's entry to the task, middle and main task. The numbers coincide, the roles do not, so personal readings are not carried over to the couple.

faq.q: Why do such couples have The Devil at the centre?
faq.a: That is how the numbers fall: in 83.9% of couples with this tail the centre is 15. A personal matrix never has centre 15, so this is an atmosphere only two people together can create. It speaks of the strength of attachment, of the feeling that the meeting was fate. The task is to keep the bond from becoming a cage: nobody belongs to anybody.

faq.q: How common is tail 9-12-3 among couples?
faq.a: Roughly one couple in 75: 1.334% of all couples, 25th place among the 97 possible couple tails. It is built from six combinations of the partners' personal tails, most often 9-3-21 and 18-9-9.

Chekhov places houses all through it: Gurov "owned two houses in Moscow", Anna Sergeyevna's husband "lived in a house of his own". Each of them has a house; the couple has a hotel room. The Empress's task here lies not in walls but in visibility: **there has to be somewhere the union can be seen.**

A visible home takes many forms: a flat, even a rented one, with both names on the door; a shared budget instead of "my" money and "your" money; a party the two of them throw for their people; a shared venture that grows; a plan with dates instead of "some day". Through the minus the task is just as recognisable: years together and not a single shared shelf; one grows at work while the other waits and stores up resentment; the parents still decide where the couple sees in the New Year. Neither of the two has The Empress as a personal task: the most earthly card in the deck is one the couple only gets together.

Four years before the story he wrote to Suvorin: "give me a wife who, like the moon, won't appear in my sky every day". Six years later, having married Olga Knipper, he sent his mother a telegram: "Dear Mama, give me your blessing, I am getting married. Everything will stay as it was. Leaving to drink koumiss." **"Everything will stay as it was" is The Hermit's wish in the role of resistance:** a family begins with a promise that nothing will begin. And the story ends with the words "a new and splendid life would begin". Between those two phrases lies the whole of The Empress's task.

In Yalta Chekhov had a garden, and Kuprin remembered how "in the mornings, alone, silently, he trimmed his roses, still moist from the dew". Alone and silent — that is The Hermit. A garden that has begun to bear fruit — that is The Empress. One picture holds the strong version of the tail: a silence that grows something. All a 9-12-3 couple has to do is change one word — not "alone" but "together" — and instead of "the solution would be found", say "we decided".

unit.title: From secret to a visible home

captions.M: To want a world for two, and quiet
captions.N: To live “for the time being” for years, awaiting a decision
captions.D: To give the union a visible home, budget and plans

unit.meaning: Your task is to stop waiting for the solution to turn up by itself, say “we decided” and give your union a visible home.
